newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Beaten Singapore opposition leader to take seat.
newsitem.headline: Beaten Singapore opposition leader to take seat.

text.p: Combative Singapore opposition leader Joshua Jeyaretnam, beaten in parliamentary elections earlier this month, will take a seat in the assembly anyway, his party announced on Friday.
The Workers' Party said in a statement Jeyaretnam would take up the constitutionally-provided seat for the "best loser" despite the party's opposition to the provision.

The veteran politician, who in 1981 became the first opposition candidate to win a seat in parliament after independence, was on a five-man slate in the multi-member, winner-take-all constituency of Cheng San in January 2 elections.

Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong's long-dominant People's Action Party (PAP) won the bitterly fought contest with 55 percent of the vote, well below the overall 65 percent share that won it all but two of the contested seats in the 83-member parliament.
The constitution provides for the best loser to be given a so-called non-constituency seat, which carries limited voting rights, if the opposition wins fewer than three seats.
Jeyaretnam's presence in parliament promises some lively debates.
He became the first person to break the PAP's monopoly on power when he won election to parliament in 1981, and retained his seat in 1984 polls.

Jeyaretnam's verbal jousts in parliament with then Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew became the stuff of legend as Jeyaretnam launched blistering accusations that the government was curtailing civil liberties and freedom of the press.
Over the years, he paid more than Singapore $780,000 (US$557,000) to Lee for libel.
Real trouble for Jeyaretnam began shortly after he was re-elected in 1984.

In November 1986, the High Court sentenced Jeyaretnam and then Workers' Party chairman Wong Hong Tay to one month in jail and fined them S$5,000 (US$3,570) each on charges of making false statements about the party's accounts.
The conviction disqualified Jeyaretnam from serving in parliament and barred him from contesting for five years.
He appealed to the Privy Council in London, the highest court for many Commonwealth nations, and won a widely publicised condemnation of what had happened.
The council said "that by a series of misjudgments the appellant and his co-accused Wong have suffered a grievous injustice".
Their subsequent request for a presidential pardon was turned down.
The Workers' Party statement on Friday said it remained committed to the abolition of the non-constituency seat but would take it anyway because of the way Goh campaigned in Cheng San.

Goh told voters that an opposition victory would mean they went to the back of the queue for a multi-billion dollar government housing renovation scheme, a tactic which brought criticism from the U.S. State Department.
The Workers' Party statement said its executive council believed voters were intimidated by Goh's campaign.

"The council also felt that to refuse to take up the seat would do an injustice to the 45 percent of the voters in Cheng San who wished to be heard in parliament through the candidates of the Workers' Party."
